page.title: Best Amplifier for a Passive Subwoofer (2026): 4 Picks by Setup
page.h1: Best amplifier for a passive subwoofer
page.desc: The best amplifier for a passive subwoofer, sorted by setup: receiver with a sub out, 2.1 bookshelf systems, amps with no sub out and big home-theater subs.
page.intro:
Short answer. The best amplifier for a passive subwoofer is the Fosi Audio M03 ({buy:fosi-audio-m03-subwoofer-amplifier}) if your receiver or amp has a sub out. It is a TPA3255 mono amp for 4–8 Ω subs, with a low-pass knob that covers the usual 80–120 Hz crossover and a 32 V power supply in the box. If one amp has to run passive bookshelf speakers and a passive sub, get the Fosi BT30D Pro ({buy:fosi-audio-bt30d-pro}): two TPA3255 chips, a separate sub channel with 0–300 Hz SUB FREQ and SUB VOL knobs, and support for 2–8 Ω loads.

Expect less power than the box says. Owners and reviewers complain about this more than anything else. One reviewer estimated the BT30D Pro's “350 W” sub channel at about 100 W on the stock 32 V supply. That is fine for a small room, but not for a 15-inch home-theater sub.

Two cases where neither Fosi amp is the right buy. If your stereo amp has no sub out, the Dayton Audio SA100 is the better fit: it takes speaker-level inputs, has auto-on and phase control, and carries a 5-year warranty. For a big home-theater sub, the Dayton Audio SA1000DSP has the power (311 W × 2 at 4 Ω, more than 1,000 W bridged) and auto room EQ.

page.after:
What owners complain about

  • Power that isn't there. This came up most often. Small class-D amps list peak numbers, and the 32 V supplies that ship with them cap output. One reviewer heard about 40–50 W per speaker and about 100 W to the sub from the BT30D Pro's “165 W × 2 + 350 W.”
  • No auto-on, or a standby that misbehaves. Many small sub amps have only a power switch. Fosi's M03 page lists no auto-on. If that matters, the Dayton SA100 and SA1000DSP turn on when they detect a signal.
  • Pops and hum. Owners report pops at power-on or power-off on several amps, including a small click when the BT30D Pro turns off. Dayton's SA100 manual says hum can still occur. Turn the gain down before you power on.
  • Crossover confusion. The BT30D Pro's SUB FREQ knob has no markings. If your receiver already sets the sub crossover (bass management), turn the amp's low-pass all the way up so the two filters don't stack.
  • 3 Ω subs from old home-theater sets. The BT30D Pro is rated for 2–8 Ω. The M03 is rated for 4–8 Ω.

Which one by need

  • Receiver or amp with a sub (LFE) out: Fosi M03 ({buy:fosi-audio-m03-subwoofer-amplifier}).
  • Passive bookshelf speakers plus a passive sub, one amp, Bluetooth: Fosi BT30D Pro ({buy:fosi-audio-bt30d-pro}).
  • Stereo amp with no sub out: Dayton Audio SA100, which uses speaker-level in and out.
  • Same 2.1 job, longest warranty: Dayton Audio DTA-2.1BT2. It has less power than the BT30D Pro but a 5-year warranty.
  • Large home-theater sub: Dayton Audio SA1000DSP.

Not recommended

  • Amps whose “sub out” is an RCA or 3.5 mm jack. That is a line-level signal for a powered sub. A passive sub needs an amplified output, such as the BT30D Pro's sub terminals, or a separate amp like the M03.
  • Fosi MC351, if you want a remote. Its spec sheet lists none, and a Fosi community reviewer found that its auto-standby did not work.

notes: QUERY: Google autocomplete for 'amplifier for passive subwoofer' returned 'best amplifier for passive subwoofer', '2.1 amplifier for passive subwoofer', 'mini…', 'external…', '…home theater', 'power amplifier…'. The SERP is thin: desertcart and spam listings, AI-written roundups (ovrclock, requirementspc) and forum threads, with no measured head-to-head. PAIN POINTS (counted across about 14 reviews, manuals and threads read): inflated power ratings or a PSU capping output, 6 (AudioReviews BT30D Pro, ovrclock ×4 entries, Fosi community MC351, plus owner snippets saying the 32 V adapter isn't enough); no auto-on or broken standby, 6 (ovrclock ×4, MC351 community review, SA100 manual's 15–20 min standby); pops or hum, 6 (ovrclock ×3, BT30D Pro turn-off click, SA100 Audioholics hum thread, SA100 turn-on pop review); crossover issues (unmarked knob, stacked filters, missing sub controls), 5 (AudioReviews, ovrclock, MC351 reply, two Polk/Audioholics double-filter threads); 3 Ω HTiB subs, 3 (Stereonet, diyaudio, Tom's Guide); heat, 3 (AudioReviews plus a commenter on the BT30D Pro, MC351 buyer). SEGMENT WINNERS: (1) receiver or amp with a sub pre-out: Fosi M03 at $76.49, the lowest-cost TPA3255 sub amp with a low-pass and PSU included, vs Dayton SA100 at about $148 at Parts Express by snippet (not verified; Parts Express page returned empty). (2) one amp for passive bookshelf speakers plus a passive sub: Fosi BT30D Pro at $109.99. It has two TPA3255 chips vs the Dayton DTA-2.1BT2's TPA3116 (50 W × 2 + 100 W), plus a separate SUB VOL and a 0–300 Hz crossover; the Dayton's advantages are a 5-year warranty and a 50–120 Hz marked crossover. (3) stereo amp with no sub out: Dayton SA100 wins on speaker-level in/out, auto-on, phase and a 5-year warranty; Fosi has no speaker-level-input sub amp. (4) big home-theater subs: Dayton SA1000DSP. Dayton products are named without links per the 2026-11-06 Amazon-walled rule, with no prices. PRICES verified on fosiaudio.com 2026-11-10 with storecheck: M03 $76.49 (compare $89.99, available, single variant, 32 V/5 A included); BT30D Pro + 32 V/5 A $109.99 (available), BT30D Pro + 48 V/5 A $139.99 (Fosi says it needs active cooling). The store rate-limited heavily (HTTP 429), so I re-read after waiting. UNVERIFIED / KEPT OFF THE PAGE OR HEDGED: the M03's true rated power (Fosi's own page says both 150 W and 200 W at 4 Ω; Audiophonics says 120 W); the M03 low-pass range (20–200 vs 20–300 Hz, so the page says only that it covers 80–120 Hz); whether the M03 accepts 48 V (the Fosi US page says 24–48 V DC, Audiophonics says 24–36 V); M03 discontinuation (Audiophonics and ExtremeHiFi say discontinued, the US store shows it in stock; it may sell out); BT30D Pro warranty (the Fosi instruction page says 18 months in one section and 24 months elsewhere); the BT30D Pro DC input range (the FAQ says 12–36 V, yet Fosi sells a 48 V bundle); the 'about 100 W to the sub' figure is one reviewer's listening estimate, not a bench measurement; a snippet claiming 75 W clipping on the sub channel could not be tied to the Pro model, so I left it out. Dayton SA1000DSP bridged power conflicts on Dayton's own page (1,150 vs 1,208 W). CODES: Fosi lists no Awin codes. The only code on fosiaudio.com was IFAFOSI on a German-language IFA 2026 page (new-subscriber, probably expired), and I could not see a current US banner because of rate limits, so I listed none. Coupon-site codes (AVA, WETHRIFT15, TPDMAX) were ignored. OTHER FOSI PRODUCTS CONSIDERED: MC351 (2.1 with optical/USB, $169.99 without PSU / $189.99 with 32 V / $209.99 with 48 V) was dropped as a pick because it has no remote and the community reviewer reported broken auto-standby and missing sub controls. M04 is out of stock in the US ($53.99). M01-BT is $89.99 (not evaluated in depth).
